meta.blurb: A boy knocks at the house of Death and will not leave without an answer. In the Upanishads, the great dialogues of ancient India, students ask what the mind is, what happens after death, and who we really are.
meta.bible: Upanishads: ancient Sanskrit texts of India, part of Hindu scripture, usually dated to about the eighth century BCE and later. Sanskrit: the old language of India. Hindu. India. Vedas: the oldest sacred hymns, which the Upanishads end. Brahman: the one ultimate reality behind the world. Atman: the Self, the innermost being of each person. Self: the deepest part of a person, the same as Brahman according to the texts. Om: the sacred sound. Isha: the short Upanishad that begins with the Lord filling all things. Kena: the Upanishad whose first word means by whom. Agni: god of fire. Vayu: god of wind. Indra: king of the gods. Uma: a radiant woman, daughter of the Himalaya, who names Brahman. Himalaya. Katha: the Upanishad of Nachiketa. Vajashravas: Nachiketa's father. Nachiketa: a boy sent to Death by his father. Yama: the lord of death. Prashna: the Upanishad of six questions. Pippalada: the sage who answers them. Mundaka: the Upanishad of two kinds of knowledge. Shaunaka: the householder who asks. Angiras: the teacher who answers. Satyameva Jayate: Sanskrit for truth alone triumphs, now the motto of India. Devanagari: the script used for Sanskrit. Mandukya: the shortest of the main ones, twelve verses on Om. Turiya: the fourth state, beyond waking, dreaming and deep sleep. Taittiriya: the Upanishad of the five sheaths and of the teacher's last advice. Bhrigu: the son who asks. Varuna: his father. Chandogya: the Upanishad of Shvetaketu. Shvetaketu: a proud student. Uddalaka: his father and teacher. Tat Tvam Asi: Sanskrit for you are that. Satyakama Jabala: a boy who tells the truth. Jabala: his mother. Gautama: the teacher who accepts him. Prajapati: the creator, who teaches Indra and the demon Virochana. Virochana. Brihadaranyaka: the great forest Upanishad, the longest. Yajnavalkya: the great sage. Maitreyi and Katyayani: his two wives. Gargi: a woman scholar. Janaka: a king who loves learning. Neti Neti: Sanskrit for not this, not this. Shvetashvatara: the Upanishad that speaks of God as a person. Aitareya: the Upanishad of creation. Shankara: the philosopher of about the eighth century CE who wrote commentaries. Ramanuja: a later teacher who read the texts differently. Dara Shikoh: a Mughal prince who had them put into Persian about 1657. Mughal. Persian. Latin. Europe. Arthur Schopenhauer: a German philosopher who read them. Da: the thunder's single sound. Voice and tone: calm, clear, respectful and warm. Every idea is attributed to the text it comes from. The words are retold, never long quotations. Where scholars disagree, say so. Never preach or compare traditions unkindly.

beats.scene: A teacher and students sit in a circle under a forest tree
beats.summary: The Upanishads are introduced as ancient Sanskrit texts of India.

beats.scene: Young students sit close around an old teacher on a woven mat
beats.summary: The word Upanishad is explained as sitting down near a teacher.

beats.scene: One flame is reflected in many small clay lamps in a dark room
beats.summary: The central idea is that one reality, Brahman, is the same as the Self, Atman.

beats.scene: A sage stands on a hill at dawn and looks out over fields
beats.summary: The Isha Upanishad begins by saying that the Lord fills everything, so enjoy by letting go.

beats.scene: A farmer works his field at sunrise with a calm face
beats.summary: The Isha says to keep working, and that one who sees the Self in all beings feels no hatred.

beats.scene: The bright sun glows behind a golden disc above a hill
beats.summary: A verse asks the sun to remove the golden disc that hides the face of truth.

beats.scene: A young student asks his teacher a question beside a quiet pond
beats.summary: The Kena Upanishad begins with a student asking who sends the mind to think.

beats.scene: A teacher points gently to a student's ear and eye
beats.summary: The teacher answers that Brahman is the ear of the ear and the eye of the eye.

beats.scene: Proud gods stand in a crowd as a strange glowing being appears
beats.summary: The gods win a victory and boast, so Brahman appears before them as a mysterious being.

beats.scene: A single blade of grass lies on the ground before a glowing figure
beats.summary: Agni cannot burn a blade of grass and Vayu cannot blow it away.

beats.scene: A radiant woman stands among snowy mountain peaks and speaks to Indra
beats.summary: Uma tells Indra the stranger was Brahman, and the gods learn humility.

beats.scene: A boy watches his father give away thin and tired old cows
beats.summary: In the Katha Upanishad, Nachiketa sees his father give worthless gifts and is sent to Death.

beats.scene: A boy waits alone on the dark steps of a stone house at night
beats.summary: Nachiketa waits three days at the house of Yama, who offers three wishes.

beats.scene: A boy kneels before a tall figure as a small sacred fire burns
beats.summary: Nachiketa's first two wishes: his father's calm, and the knowledge of a fire ritual.

beats.scene: Yama frowns thoughtfully as the boy asks a question in the shadows
beats.summary: Nachiketa's third wish is to know what happens after death, and Yama offers wealth instead.

beats.scene: A boy turns away from piles of gold, cattle and fine jewels
beats.summary: Nachiketa refuses all riches, saying they last only until tomorrow.

beats.scene: A path splits in two, one bright with flowers and one plain
beats.summary: Yama teaches that there are two paths, the good and the pleasant.

beats.scene: Yama and Nachiketa sit together as a soft light fills the room
beats.summary: Yama teaches that the Self is never born and never dies.

beats.scene: A chariot with white horses stands on a road at sunset
beats.summary: Yama compares a person to a chariot, with the Self as its rider.

beats.scene: A narrow path like a blade climbs a bright mountain at dawn
beats.summary: The path to the Self is as sharp as a razor, and Nachiketa is freed from fear of death.

beats.scene: Speech, eye, ear and mind argue while one calm figure rises
beats.summary: In the Prashna Upanishad, the powers of the body quarrel until the life-breath proves chief.

beats.scene: A student kneels before a teacher who holds a lamp beside scrolls
beats.summary: The Mundaka distinguishes the lower knowledge from the higher knowledge of the imperishable.

beats.scene: A spider sits at the centre of its web in the morning light
beats.summary: The Mundaka compares the world's rising from the imperishable to a spider spinning its thread.

beats.scene: Two birds sit on one branch, one eating fruit and one watching
beats.summary: The two birds on one tree stand for the self that acts and the Self that watches.

beats.scene: A road of stone steps rises up a hillside towards a bright shrine
beats.summary: Truth alone triumphs, a line later chosen as the motto of India.

beats.scene: An archer draws a bow at dawn with a steady, calm face
beats.summary: Om is the bow, the self is the arrow and Brahman is the target.

beats.scene: Many rivers flow together into a wide, still sea at sunset
beats.summary: As rivers flow into the sea and lose their names, the wise reach the highest being.

beats.scene: A hermit sits by a river and chants a deep sound at dawn
beats.summary: The Mandukya Upanishad begins by saying that Om is all this.

beats.scene: A person sleeps, dreams and wakes, while a calm light stays still
beats.summary: Waking, dreaming and deep sleep are three states, and the fourth, Turiya, lies beyond them.

beats.scene: A young man sits in meditation under a tree while his father watches
beats.summary: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, Bhrigu seeks Brahman through effort and finds it in five layers.

beats.scene: A graduate bows to his teacher at the door of a forest school
beats.summary: At the end of their study, a teacher gives his students advice for life.

beats.scene: A proud young man in fine clothes stands before his father holding clay
beats.summary: Shvetaketu returns proud from twelve years of study, and his father shows him that knowing one thing can mean knowing all.

beats.scene: A boy splits a small fruit open under a huge banyan tree
beats.summary: A banyan seed holds an unseen essence from which the great tree grows: Tat Tvam Asi.

beats.scene: A boy sips water from a clay bowl as his father watches
beats.summary: Salt dissolved in water cannot be seen, but it is in every sip.

beats.scene: A boy speaks honestly to a seated teacher about his mother
beats.summary: Satyakama tells the truth about his birth, and the teacher Gautama accepts him.

beats.scene: Two figures look at their reflections in a bowl of water before a sage
beats.summary: Indra and Virochana learn about the Self from Prajapati, but only Indra keeps asking.

beats.scene: A man sits in a dark room as a single lamp slowly brightens
beats.summary: The Brihadaranyaka's prayer asks to be led from the unreal to the real.

beats.scene: A woman and her husband sit by an oil lamp with bundles
beats.summary: Maitreyi asks Yajnavalkya for knowledge rather than wealth.

beats.scene: A woman scholar stands up to question a sage in a royal assembly
beats.summary: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya on what the world is woven upon.

beats.scene: A king sits by a lamp at night and questions a sage
beats.summary: Yajnavalkya tells King Janaka that when the sun, moon and fire are gone, the Self is a person's light.

beats.scene: A traveller stands before a veiled doorway made of mist
beats.summary: Yajnavalkya says the Self can only be described as not this, not this.

beats.scene: A wise man stands under a night sky full of stars and speaks
beats.summary: The Shvetashvatara asks what the world comes from and speaks to all of the great light.

beats.scene: A bright figure looks across a dark empty sea before the world begins
beats.summary: The Aitareya Upanishad says that in the beginning there was only the Self, which thought of creating the worlds.

beats.scene: Four lamps burn in a row, each in a separate little window
beats.summary: Later teachers chose four short sayings, the great sayings, to sum up the Upanishads.

beats.scene: A young monk writes on palm leaves while students listen nearby
beats.summary: Shankara wrote commentaries on the main Upanishads, and other teachers read them differently.

beats.scene: Old translated books lie open on a desk beside a candle
beats.summary: The Upanishads were translated into Persian and Latin and read in Europe.

beats.scene: Students of many ages read the same old book together in a bright room
beats.summary: The Upanishads are still chanted, studied and discussed today.

beats.scene: Dark thunderclouds roll over a hill as three groups look up
beats.summary: The thunder says Da, Da, Da to gods, humans and demons.

beats.scene: Students and a teacher sit side by side, singing at sunrise
beats.summary: Many Upanishads begin or end with a prayer for peace shared by teacher and student.

beats.scene: A student sits alone at sunrise and looks over a quiet valley
beats.summary: The Upanishads end as an invitation to sit near, ask and look inward.

B1B2: The Upanishads are ancient texts from India, written in the old language called Sanskrit. The oldest of them are usually dated to roughly the eighth to sixth centuries BCE, although scholars cannot give exact dates.
The word Upanishad is often explained as sitting down close to a teacher. Students would gather around a wise person and ask the deepest questions they could think of.
Their central idea is that there is one ultimate reality, called Brahman, behind everything in the world. The deepest self inside each person, called Atman, is said to be the same as Brahman.
The Isha Upanishad begins by saying that the Lord fills everything that moves in the world. So one should enjoy life by letting go, and should not want what belongs to others.
The Isha Upanishad tells people to go on working, even if they hope to live a hundred years. It adds that anyone who sees every creature in the Self, and the Self in every creature, feels no hatred.
One verse says that the face of truth is hidden behind a golden disc. The speaker prays to the sun, the nourisher, to remove it so that he can see the truth clearly.
The Kena Upanishad takes its name from its first word, which means by whom. A student asks who sends the mind to think, who makes the voice speak, and who makes the eyes and ears work.
The teacher answers that Brahman is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind and the eye of the eye. It cannot be described in words, but it is what makes speech possible.
Once the gods won a great victory, and they believed that the glory was theirs alone. Brahman knew this, so it appeared before them as a strange and glowing being that they did not recognise.
Agni says he can burn anything on earth, but the stranger sets down a single blade of grass. Agni uses all his power and cannot burn it, and the wind god Vayu then fails to blow it away.

Indra, the king of the gods, goes up to the stranger, but it vanishes before him. In its place stands Uma, a radiant woman, who explains that the stranger was Brahman and that the victory was Brahman's.
In the Katha Upanishad, a man named Vajashravas gives gifts at a great ritual, but the cows he offers are old and weak. His young son Nachiketa sees this and worries that the gift is empty.
Nachiketa goes to the house of Yama, the lord of death, but Yama is away. The boy waits at the door for three days and nights without food or water.

For his first wish, Nachiketa asks that his father may stop being angry and greet him happily when he returns. For his second, he asks to learn about a sacred fire ritual that leads to heaven, and Yama teaches it gladly.

For his third wish, Nachiketa asks what happens after death, since some say that a person continues and others say not. Yama replies that even the gods once doubted this, and he begs the boy to ask for something else.

Nachiketa refuses every offer, because all these pleasures last only until tomorrow and wear out our senses. Wealth can never make a man happy, he says, and he will not choose anything but his third wish.
Yama is impressed, and he explains that there are two paths, the good and the pleasant. The wise choose the good, while foolish people choose the pleasant because they want comfort and possessions.
Yama teaches that the Self, the knower within, is never born and never dies. It does not come from anything and it does not become anything, and it is not killed even when the body is killed.
Yama gives a famous picture in which the Self is the rider of a chariot and the body is the chariot itself. The mind is like the reins, the understanding is the driver, and the senses are the horses.

Yama says that the path to the Self is as sharp as the edge of a razor, and hard to walk. He calls out, arise, awake, and seek good teachers, and Nachiketa learns the truth and is freed from fear of death.

In the Prashna Upanishad, six seekers each ask the sage Pippalada a deep question. In one answer, speech, mind, sight and hearing argue about which is greatest, until the life-breath starts to leave and pulls them along.

In the Mundaka Upanishad, a householder named Shaunaka asks the teacher Angiras what one thing must be known in order to know everything. Angiras replies that there are two kinds of knowledge, the lower and the higher.

The Mundaka says that as a spider sends out its thread and draws it back, so the world comes from the imperishable. Plants grow from the earth and hair grows from the body in the same way, the text adds.
The Mundaka Upanishad pictures two birds, close friends, sitting on the same tree. One eats the sweet and bitter fruit, while the other simply watches and does not eat.
The Mundaka says that truth alone wins, and not falsehood. These words, in Sanskrit, were later chosen as the national motto of India, and they are written beneath the national emblem.
The Mundaka says that Om is the bow and the self is the arrow. The target is Brahman, and the archer must take careful aim with a steady mind, so that the arrow becomes one with its mark.

As rivers flow into the sea and give up their names and shapes, the wise person reaches the highest divine person, says the Mundaka. Whoever knows the highest Brahman, the text declares, becomes Brahman himself.
The Mandukya Upanishad is very short, yet many readers treat it as one of the deepest. It begins by saying that the sound Om is all this, the past, the present and the future.
The Mandukya describes waking, dreaming and deep sleep as three states of a person. Beyond them lies a fourth, called Turiya, which is peaceful and is said to be the Self itself.

In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a young man named Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him about Brahman. Varuna sets him a task, and the son finds Brahman first in food, then in breath, mind, understanding and joy.

At the end of their study, a teacher gives his students his final advice. Speak the truth, do your duty, never stop learning, and treat your mother, your father, your teacher and your guests as if they were gods.

In the Chandogya Upanishad, young Shvetaketu returns home after twelve years of study, very proud of his learning. His father Uddalaka asks if he has learned how to hear what cannot be heard, and Shvetaketu has no answer.

Uddalaka asks his son to split open a small fruit from a banyan tree, and then one of its tiny seeds. Inside he sees nothing at all, yet his father says that the great tree grows from that unseen essence.
Uddalaka tells his son to put a lump of salt in water and come back in the morning. The salt cannot be seen, yet every sip of the water tastes of it, and the Self is like that.

Young Satyakama asks his mother Jabala for his father's name, and she tells him honestly that she does not know. He repeats this to the teacher Gautama, who says that only a truthful boy would dare to say it, and accepts him as a pupil.

The god Indra and the demon Virochana study for thirty-two years with Prajapati, who tells them to look at themselves in a bowl of water. Virochana is happy with the body and leaves, but Indra sees that the body decays, so he comes back to ask again.

The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, whose name means great forest teaching, is the longest of all. One of its best-loved prayers asks to be led from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, and from death to immortality.

The sage Yajnavalkya decides to leave home and divides his goods between his two wives. His wife Maitreyi asks whether wealth could make her immortal, and when he says no, she asks him to teach her what he knows.

At King Janaka's great gathering of scholars, a woman named Gargi asks the sage Yajnavalkya what the whole world is woven upon. He answers from water to air to the highest worlds until he reaches Brahman, and then he warns her that no question can go further.
King Janaka asks Yajnavalkya what a person uses as a light. The sage names the sun, the moon, fire and speech, but when all of these are gone, the Self is the light that remains.
Yajnavalkya says that the Self can only be described as not this, not this. You cannot see the seer of seeing, he explains, nor hear the hearer of hearing.

The Shvetashvatara Upanishad begins with questions about what the world comes from: time, nature, chance, or something more. Later it calls out to all people, saying that it knows the great Person, bright as the sun, beyond all darkness.

The Aitareya Upanishad says that in the beginning there was only the Self, and it thought, let me create the worlds. After the worlds were made, the Self entered the person it had created and became the one who knows.
Later teachers chose four short sentences from the texts, called the great sayings. They are consciousness is Brahman, this Self is Brahman, you are that, and I am Brahman.

Many centuries later, a teacher named Shankara wrote long commentaries on the main Upanishads, probably in the eighth century CE. He taught that Brahman alone is real, while later teachers such as Ramanuja read the texts differently.

In the 1650s, a Mughal prince named Dara Shikoh had the Upanishads translated into Persian. A Latin version made from it, in the early 1800s, was read in Europe by the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer, who admired it greatly.

Today the Upanishads are still chanted, studied and discussed, in schools, temples and homes around the world. Readers of many backgrounds turn to them with questions about the self, death, truth and the meaning of life.

In a short story, gods, humans and demons ask the creator for advice, and he answers each of them with the single sound Da. The gods hear self-control, humans hear giving, and demons hear compassion, and the thunder still repeats the lesson.
Many Upanishads begin or end with a short prayer for peace. One asks that teacher and student may be protected together, may work together, and may never come to hate each other.

The Upanishads do not offer a list of rules so much as an invitation to look inward. Like Nachiketa and Shvetaketu, the reader is asked to sit near the teacher, ask without fear, and discover what is true.
C1C2: The Upanishads are among the oldest philosophical and spiritual writings of India, composed in Sanskrit by many unnamed teachers over several centuries. The earliest are usually dated to roughly the eighth to sixth centuries before the common era, although scholars admit that exact dates cannot be known. They belong to the Hindu tradition, which holds them in deep reverence as part of its sacred literature.

The word Upanishad is traditionally understood to mean sitting down near, a phrase that pictures a student gathered close to a teacher to receive a private teaching. Many of the texts are written as conversations, in which a pupil, a king or a wife asks the question that has been troubling her or him. The form itself is a lesson, for it suggests that wisdom is found by asking, listening and thinking together.

At the heart of the Upanishads stands the idea of Brahman, the single ultimate reality that underlies and sustains the whole universe. Atman, the innermost self of every living being, is declared to be none other than Brahman, a claim that the texts return to again and again. Later teachers explained that unity in different ways, and this book simply follows the texts as they speak.

The Isha Upanishad, one of the shortest of all, opens by declaring that the Lord dwells within everything that moves in this changing world. From this it draws a gentle rule of life: enjoy what you have by giving up the grasping, and do not covet the wealth of anyone else. A person who sees the divine everywhere, it suggests, has no need to take more than is needed.

Do not run away from the world, the Isha Upanishad advises, but go on doing your work through a long life without letting the work bind you. It teaches that whoever sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, no longer shrinks from anyone in fear or contempt. Seeing the same life everywhere, in other words, is the root of a quiet and fearless compassion.

In one of its best-loved verses, the Isha Upanishad says that the face of truth is covered by a golden disc, which most readers take to be the blinding brightness of the sun. The speaker begs the sun, the great nourisher of the world, to draw back its dazzling light so that he may at last see what lies behind it. The prayer expresses a longing familiar to many traditions, the wish to look through the shining surface of things to the reality beneath.

The Kena Upanishad takes its name from its opening word, which means by whom, and it begins with a pupil's sweeping question about the source of human life. By whom, he asks, is the mind sent out to think, by whom does the breath first move, and who makes the voice speak and the eye and ear perceive? The question is bold because it treats everyday abilities, which most of us take for granted, as a mystery worth investigating.

The teacher replies in a famous riddle: Brahman is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speech of speech and the eye of the eye. It cannot be grasped by words, he says, because words themselves are lit by it, and it cannot be seen by sight, because it is what makes sight possible. Those who truly understand this, the text promises, are set free from sorrow and become immortal.

The Kena Upanishad tells a story in which the gods win a great victory over their enemies and begin to boast that the triumph belongs to them alone. Brahman, knowing the secret of their pride, appears before them in the form of a mysterious being whom none of them can name. The gods are uneasy, and they send Agni, the god of fire, to find out who this stranger is.

The fire god Agni boasts that he can burn anything in the world, but when the stranger lays down a single blade of grass, all his blazing power cannot consume it. The wind god Vayu, who claims that he can sweep away anything at all, tries next and cannot stir the blade even slightly. Humbled, both return to the others and admit that they cannot tell what this being is.

When Indra himself goes to question the mysterious being, it vanishes, and in its place he finds a radiant woman named Uma, a daughter of the Himalaya. She tells him that the stranger was Brahman, and that the victory they had been so proud of had really been won by Brahman's power. In that moment the gods learn humility, and the story teaches that no strength, however great, belongs to the one who uses it.

The Katha Upanishad begins with a father, Vajashravas, who performs a great ritual and gives away cows so old and weak that they can no longer give milk. His young son Nachiketa, who has faith that the gifts must be worthy, asks his father again and again who will receive him. Losing his temper at last, the father snaps that he will give the boy to Death.

Obedient to his father's words, Nachiketa travels to the house of Yama, the lord of death, only to find that Yama is not at home. For three days and three nights the boy waits at the door without eating, and the tradition holds that a guest who is neglected brings misfortune on the house. When Yama returns he is ashamed, and he offers the boy three wishes to make amends for the delay.

Nachiketa's first wish is a loving one: that his father's anger may fade, and that he may welcome his son home with joy when he returns from the house of Death. His second wish is to be taught the fire ritual that leads to heaven, and Yama explains it so clearly, and is so pleased with the boy's quick understanding, that he names the fire after him. Only the third wish remains, and it is the one that the whole Upanishad has been waiting to hear.

Nachiketa's third wish is the hardest of all: he asks to know what becomes of a person after death, for some say that the soul continues, and others say that it does not. Yama, who knows the answer better than anyone, tells him that even the gods once doubted this subtle matter, and he urges the boy to choose another gift. He offers sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years, herds of cattle, gold, a long life, and every pleasure that the earth can give.

Nachiketa refuses every one of these treasures, answering that they are fleeting, that they wear out the senses, and that life is short at best. Wealth, he says, can never truly satisfy a person, and having met Death himself, he will not ask for any gift except the knowledge he first requested. The young boy's steadiness, which no bribe can shake, is what convinces Yama that he is ready to hear the truth.

Delighted, Yama begins to teach, and his first lesson is that there are two paths open to every person, the path of what is good and the path of what is pleasant. The wise, he says, look carefully at both and choose the good, whereas the foolish, driven by the hunger for comfort and possession, choose what is merely pleasant. He praises Nachiketa because the boy was not tempted by pleasant things, even when they were laid out before him.

The heart of Yama's teaching is that the Self, the wise knower within, is never born and never dies, and that it has not come from anywhere or turned into anything. It is unborn, constant and ancient, and it is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. Smaller than the smallest thing and greater than the greatest, it is hidden in the heart of every creature, and the person who is free from desire and sorrow may catch sight of it.

Yama offers a famous comparison in which the Self is the master riding in a chariot, the body is the chariot, and the intellect is the charioteer who steers. The mind holds the reins, the senses are the horses, and the roads they run along are the objects of desire. A driver who lacks understanding is dragged along by wild horses, but a wise and steady one brings the chariot safely to the end of its journey.

The path to the Self, says Yama, is as sharp as a razor's edge and difficult to cross, and the wise call it hard. Yet he urges every listener to arise, to awake, and to seek out great teachers so that the path may be understood. Having received this knowledge from Death himself, Nachiketa, the text concludes, became free of sorrow and of the fear of dying, as will anyone who comes to know the Self in the same way.

The Prashna Upanishad, whose name means question, tells of six seekers who spend a year with the sage Pippalada in study and discipline before being allowed to ask him anything. One of them asks about the powers that hold up the body, and the sage answers with a story in which speech, mind, sight and hearing each claim that they alone sustain life. When the life-breath makes as if to leave, they are all dragged out of place like bees following their queen, and they bow to the breath as the chief.

In the Mundaka Upanishad, the householder Shaunaka approaches the teacher Angiras with a bold question: what is it that, once known, makes everything else known? Angiras answers that there are two kinds of knowledge, the lower, which includes the sacred hymns, grammar and the sciences, and the higher, by which the imperishable is realised. The distinction does not scorn learning, but it reminds the student that no accumulation of facts can replace the direct understanding of the deepest reality.

To explain how the world arises, the Mundaka Upanishad offers several images: a spider sending out its thread and drawing it back again, plants springing from the earth, and hair growing from a living body. In each case something appears to come out of a source that remains itself, and so, the text suggests, the universe comes forth from the imperishable without exhausting it. These comparisons are not proofs, but they are an invitation to look at nature and notice how creation and its source belong together.

In one of the most admired images of the Upanishads, two birds, inseparable companions, sit perched on the same tree, and one of them eats the sweet and bitter fruit while the other looks on without eating. The first bird stands for the person caught up in pleasure and pain, and the second for the Self, the silent witness within. When the first bird at last sees the greatness of the other, the text says, its sorrow falls away.

Truth alone triumphs, not falsehood, declares the Mundaka Upanishad, and it adds that the path of the gods is laid out by truth, along which the sages climb to the place where truth is found. In modern times the Sanskrit words Satyameva Jayate were taken from this verse to serve as the national motto of the Republic of India. They are written in the Devanagari script beneath the lions of the national emblem.

Taking the image of an archer, the Mundaka Upanishad says that the sacred syllable Om is the bow, that the individual self is the arrow, and that Brahman is the target. The archer must draw the bow with a mind that is calm and concentrated, and take aim without carelessness, so that the arrow becomes one with its mark. Spiritual effort, the verse implies, requires the focus of an expert marksman rather than the scattered attention of an ordinary day.

The Mundaka ends with a gentle image: as flowing rivers disappear into the ocean and lose their names and forms, so the wise person, freed from name and form, reaches the supreme being beyond all things. Whoever truly knows the highest Brahman, the text declares, becomes Brahman, and passes beyond grief and beyond the stains of the world. The simile is not about disappearing but about arriving, for it describes a river that has found the place it was always travelling towards.

The Mandukya Upanishad is only twelve short verses long, and yet teachers have studied it for centuries as a compact map of the whole of reality. It opens with the declaration that the syllable Om is all this, whatever has been, whatever is now, and whatever will be in the future. Even time, it adds, is only a form of that single sound, which points to something beyond time.

The Mandukya Upanishad describes three familiar states of a person, waking, dreaming and deep dreamless sleep, and then points to a fourth, called Turiya, which is not another state beside them but the calm awareness in which they all appear. The three sounds of Om, A, U and M, are matched with the first three states, and the silence that follows the sound is matched with the fourth. For this reason Om is chanted slowly, so that the final silence can be heard.

The Taittiriya Upanishad tells of Bhrigu, who asks his father Varuna to teach him about Brahman. Varuna does not simply explain but sets him a task: to seek that from which all beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return, and to find it through quiet effort. Step by step the son recognises Brahman first as food, then as life-breath, mind and understanding, and finally as joy, which later teachers described as five layers, or sheaths, of a person.

When his students have finished their years of study, the teacher in the Taittiriya Upanishad sends them into the world with a short list of commands that has been remembered ever since. Speak the truth, follow your duty, do not neglect your study, and treat your mother, your father, your teacher and your guest as though they were divine. Give with faith and with generosity, he adds, and when you are unsure how to act, do as thoughtful, gentle and sincere people do.

In the Chandogya Upanishad, young Shvetaketu returns from twelve years of study with a high opinion of himself and of everything he has learned. His father Uddalaka asks whether he has also learned that teaching by which what is unheard becomes heard, and what is unknown becomes known, and the boy admits that he has not. Uddalaka answers with a simple example: as by knowing one lump of clay one knows everything made of clay, so by knowing the one reality, all things are known.

Uddalaka asks his son to bring him the fruit of a banyan tree, to break it open, and then to break one of its tiny seeds in two. When the boy reports that he sees nothing inside, his father replies that the huge tree stands there only because of that fine essence which he cannot see. In the same way, he says, the subtle reality behind the world is the Self of all things, and then he speaks the famous words, tat tvam asi, you are that.

To show that the Self can be present without being seen, Uddalaka asks his son to drop a lump of salt into a bowl of water and to return the next morning. The salt has disappeared from sight, but when the boy sips from the top, the middle and the bottom, each mouthful is equally salty. In the same way, says the father, the fine essence of the world is invisible, yet it fills everything, and tat tvam asi, you are that.

Satyakama, a boy who wishes to study, asks his mother Jabala for the name of his family, and she tells him honestly that she does not know, because in her youth she was busy serving in many households. When he repeats this plainly to the teacher Gautama, the sage declares that only a truthful person could speak so without shame, and accepts him as a student. The boy's name, Satyakama Jabala, therefore carries his mother's name, and the story honours both her honesty and his.

In a famous story, the god Indra and the demon Virochana come to the creator Prajapati and live as students for thirty-two years before he tells them to look at themselves in a bowl of water. Virochana is satisfied to believe that the body is the Self and goes home content, but Indra, thinking on the way, realises that the body grows old and dies, and so he returns to ask again. After many more years of discipline he learns that the true Self is deeper than the body, the dream and even deep sleep.

The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, whose name means the great forest teaching, is the longest of the principal Upanishads, and it is full of dialogues between sages, kings and families. One of its best-known prayers asks to be led from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, and from death to immortality. Chanted in homes and temples across India today, it expresses in a few words the whole movement of the search for wisdom.

When the sage Yajnavalkya decides to leave his household for a life of wandering, he offers to divide his property between his two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani. Maitreyi asks whether she would become immortal if the whole earth, filled with riches, were hers, and when he answers that wealth cannot promise this, she asks to be taught what he knows instead. Gladly he begins, telling her that husband, wife, children and wealth are dear to us not for their own sake but for the sake of the Self.

At a great gathering of scholars held by King Janaka, the learned woman Gargi stands up and asks Yajnavalkya what the whole world is woven upon, as cloth is woven on warp and weft. He answers step by step, naming water, then air, then the sky and the higher worlds, until he arrives at Brahman, beyond which no further answer can be given. When he warns her that she must not ask beyond what can be known, she falls silent, though she later speaks again to honour him as an unequalled teacher.

King Janaka, who loves wisdom, asks Yajnavalkya what a person has for light, and the sage replies that it is the sun, and when the sun has set, the moon, and when the moon has set, fire. When fire too has gone out, he continues, it is speech, and when speech is silent, it is the Self, which gives light to all the others and needs no light of its own. It is a way of saying that the awareness within us is the last and deepest source of all that we know.

When asked to describe the Self, Yajnavalkya can only say, not this, not this, for every description turns it into one more object, and the Self is the one who knows objects. You cannot see the seer of seeing, he explains, nor hear the hearer of hearing, nor think the thinker of thought, for the knower can never be fully known as a thing. This way of speaking by denial, called neti neti in Sanskrit, became one of the characteristic methods of Indian philosophy.

The Shvetashvatara Upanishad opens with a series of open questions about the origin of the world, asking whether it comes from time, from nature, from chance or from something deeper. Later it calls out to all listeners as children of immortality, declaring that its author knows the great Person who shines like the sun beyond all darkness. The text speaks of the divine as a loving and personal being as well as an impersonal reality, a theme that later devotional traditions would develop.

The Aitareya Upanishad opens with the quiet statement that in the beginning there was nothing but the Self, which looked about and found that nothing else was awake. It thought that it would send out the worlds, and so it did, and then it considered how all this could exist without itself. The text answers that the Self entered the creatures it had formed, which is why consciousness is found in every living being.

Later teachers chose four short sentences from different Upanishads, called the great sayings, to sum up the central teaching of all of them. They are consciousness is Brahman, from the Aitareya, this Self is Brahman, from the Mandukya, you are that, from the Chandogya, and I am Brahman, from the Brihadaranyaka. Each is brief enough to be memorised and slow enough to be thought about for a lifetime.

About the eighth century CE, the philosopher and monk Shankara wrote commentaries on the principal Upanishads, explaining them as a teaching that Brahman alone is ultimately real and that the Self is not different from it. Other great teachers, such as Ramanuja several centuries later, read the same texts in other ways, finding in them a God who is distinct from the souls that love him. The fact that the Upanishads can sustain such different readings is one reason they are still discussed so eagerly.

In the 1650s, a Mughal prince named Dara Shikoh, who was deeply interested in the wisdom of other traditions, had a group of scholars translate the Upanishads into Persian. In the early 1800s a Latin translation was made from that Persian text, and through it the Upanishads reached readers across Europe, including the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer. He wrote that they had been the comfort of his life, and his enthusiasm helped to spread their fame.

Today the Upanishads are still chanted by priests and students, studied in universities, and read in many languages by people who have never set foot in India. Readers of every background turn to them with the questions that never grow old: what a self is, what happens at death, what is true, and how one should live. For many Hindus they remain a living scripture, and for others they are simply some of the oldest and boldest thinking that humanity has recorded.

In a short story from the Brihadaranyaka, gods, humans and demons each come to the creator Prajapati to ask for teaching, and to each he gives a single syllable, Da. The gods understand that they should practise self-control, humans that they should give generously, and demons that they should show compassion, and the roll of thunder still repeats the same three sounds. Each group, it seems, is asked to correct the fault that comes most naturally to it.

Many Upanishads begin or end with a short prayer for peace, which is still sung before study in schools across India. One of these, found in the Katha and Taittiriya Upanishads, asks that teacher and student may be protected and nourished together, may work with great energy, may find their learning bright, and may never come to hate each other. It closes with the word for peace spoken three times, as if to calm the body, the mind and the world around.

The Upanishads do not offer a list of rules so much as an invitation, and it is the invitation of the old teacher to the pupil who has come to sit near. Like Nachiketa before Death, Shvetaketu before his father and Maitreyi before her husband, the reader is asked to question boldly, to listen carefully and to look inward for the answer. The chant that closes so many of the texts says it best, as Om, peace, peace, peace.
